subject: psychology
title: Memory: EWT & Cognitive Interview
welcome_lead: Loftus shows how a single verb can rewrite what a witness saw.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology eyewitness testimony: Loftus & Palmer 1974, anxiety, Cognitive Interview Geiselman.
final_note: Memory is reconstructive — leading questions are the prosecution's friend.

concepts.def: Eyewitness testimony — recall of a witnessed event.
A question whose form suggests a particular answer.
Talking after an event, which contaminates memory.
Anxiety narrows attention onto a weapon, away from face.
Geiselman's four-stage technique improving EWT accuracy.
Performance peaks at moderate arousal — inverted-U.

walkthroughs.body_html: Loftus & Palmer (1974) showed 45 students a car crash clip. The verb in 'about how fast were they going when they ___?' shifted estimates: 'smashed' 40.8mph, 'hit' 34.0mph. A week later, smashed-condition participants were more likely to report broken glass that wasn't there.

Anxiety has mixed effects. Johnson & Scott (1976) found weapon focus — participants who saw a knife recalled the man's face less accurately than those who saw a pen. Yet Yuille & Cutshall (1986) found real witnesses to a Vancouver shooting were highly accurate five months later, fitting the inverted-U.

The Cognitive Interview (Geiselman 1985) uses four techniques: report everything, reinstate context, reverse order, change perspective. Meta-analyses (Kohnken 1999) show ~34% more correct info than standard interviews, with little increase in errors.
